title: EITC and Child Tax Credit checker (tax year 2025)
description: Answer plain-language questions to see whether you may qualify for the federal Earned Income Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, and the credit for other dependents for tax year 2025, and roughly how much.
disclaimer: This is an estimate for information only, not tax advice and not a tax return. It covers common situations and simplifies some rules. Check IRS.gov or a free VITA tax-help site before you file.

sources.title: Public Law 119-21 (2025 reconciliation act), section 70104: Child Tax Credit

question.prompt: Which filing status will you use on your 2025 tax return?
question.help: Your filing status depends mostly on whether you were married on December 31, 2025. If you're not sure, the IRS Interactive Tax Assistant can help you pick.

options.label: Single
options.help: Not married at the end of 2025.

options.label: Head of household
options.help: Not married, and you paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying person.

options.label: Married filing jointly
options.help: Married, and you and your spouse file one return together.

options.label: Married filing separately
options.help: Married, and you each file your own return.

options.label: Qualifying surviving spouse
options.help: Your spouse died in 2023 or 2024, you didn't remarry, and you have a dependent child.

question.prompt: Can someone else claim you as a dependent on their 2025 tax return?
question.help: For example, a parent you live with who pays most of your expenses. Answer yes if someone could claim you, even if they don't.

question.prompt: Do you have a Social Security number that is valid for work?
question.help: It must be issued by the due date of your return. An ITIN doesn't count. A card that says "Valid for work only with DHS authorization" does count.

question.prompt: Were you a U.S. citizen or resident alien for all of 2025?
question.help: A resident alien has a green card or meets the IRS substantial presence test (generally, in the U.S. at least 183 days counting part of the 2 prior years).

question.prompt: Add each child or young relative who lived with you in 2025.
question.help: Include sons and daughters (including adopted), stepchildren, foster children, brothers and sisters, and their children — like grandchildren, nieces and nephews. If there's no one to add, continue with nobody listed.

question.prompt: Was {{item}} a full-time student for at least 5 months of 2025?
question.help: The months don't have to be in a row. Online-only schools may not count.

question.prompt: Is {{item}} permanently and totally disabled?
question.help: A doctor has determined {{item}} can't do any substantial work because of a physical or mental condition expected to last at least a year, or to lead to death.

question.prompt: Did {{item}} live with you for more than half of 2025?
question.help: Time away at school, on vacation, for medical care or in juvenile detention counts as living with you. A child born or who died in 2025 counts if they lived with you the whole time they were alive.

question.prompt: Is {{item}} married and filing a joint return for 2025?
question.help: Answer no if {{item}} and their spouse are filing jointly only to get back tax that was withheld.

question.prompt: Will someone else, such as {{item}}'s other parent, claim {{item}} on their 2025 return?
question.help: Only one person can claim a child for these credits. If more than one person could, the IRS tie-breaker rules usually favor the parent {{item}} lived with longest.

/children/*/supportsSelf.label: {{item}} paid for more than half of their own support

question.prompt: Did {{item}} pay for more than half of their own living expenses in 2025?
question.help: Count only money {{item}} spent on their own support, like housing, food and clothing. Money you or others spent doesn't count.

question.help: Children born in the U.S. are citizens.

/children/*/hasSsn.label: {{item}} has a Social Security number valid for work

question.prompt: Does {{item}} have a Social Security number that is valid for work?
question.help: It must be issued by the due date of your return. An ITIN or ATIN doesn't count for the Child Tax Credit or the EITC, but {{item}} may still count for the credit for other dependents.

question.prompt: How much did you earn from jobs in 2025, before taxes?
question.help: Add up box 1 of every W-2. Include tips. If you're filing jointly, include your spouse's pay. Enter 0 if none.

question.prompt: Did you work for yourself in 2025 — for example freelancing, gig work, or running a business?
question.help: Include your spouse's self-employment if you're filing jointly.

question.prompt: What were your net earnings from self-employment in 2025?
question.help: Your profit after business expenses, minus the deductible half of self-employment tax (Schedule SE). Enter a negative number for a loss.

question.prompt: How much investment income did you have in 2025?
question.help: Interest (including tax-exempt interest), dividends, capital gains, and net rental or royalty income. Enter 0 if none.

question.prompt: Did you have any other taxable income in 2025?
question.help: For example unemployment benefits, taxable retirement or pension payments, taxable Social Security, or alimony from an agreement made before 2019. Don't count child support.

question.prompt: How much other taxable income did you have in 2025?
question.help: Don't include pay from work, self-employment or investment income — you've already told us about those.

/eitc/amount.label: Earned Income Tax Credit
/eitc/amount.notes: Follows the IRS EIC table method: the credit is figured on the midpoint of each $50 income row, using the smaller of the amounts for earned income and AGI once AGI reaches the phase-out start.

explain.known: Your estimated Earned Income Tax Credit is {{/eitc/amount}}. It is refundable: you get it even if you owe no tax.
explain.zero: You don't get the Earned Income Tax Credit.
